name: English
title: Golden Harbour Games
description: An independent game studio between two harbours: Vladivostok’s Golden Horn and Sydney Harbour. We make the games we love to play, for Android, iPhone, Windows and the browser, and we experiment with VR, AR and robots.
og_description: Games from two harbours. Free on Android, iPhone, PC and in your browser.

hero.title: Games from two harbours
hero.lede: We love games, so we make the ones we want to play: small, polished and easy to pick up, whoever you are. Three are out on Android and iPhone, and every one of them plays free in your browser.

peregon.title: Range Anxiety: Far East
peregon.text: A roguelike about buying used electric cars in Vladivostok and driving them somewhere colder. The car is fine. The country is the boss.
peregon.seo_title: Range Anxiety: Far East – EV road-trip roguelike, free to play
peregon.seo_description: Buy a used electric car in Vladivostok and drive it west through the Far East winter. A browser roguelike about batteries, chargers and the cold.
intro: You run a one-person drive-away business. Cars come off the boats from Japan cheap. Buyers live west, where the chargers don’t. Every run is one car, one buyer, one road, and one battery that heat, speed, hills and the cold all come out of.

sections.title: A run, in short
list: Pick a car on the lot. Check the pack, the paint and the service book, or don’t, and find out on the road.
Plan each leg: route, speed, cabin heat. Every choice shows up as kWh before you commit.
Drive. The estimator gives you a number. Sometimes it apologises.
Stop at gas stations, cafés and dachas. The charger works, needs an app, takes cash only, has a Land Cruiser parked in front of it, or is a socket behind a counter.
Reach the buyer. He walks round the car twice. Own what’s wrong with it, talk it down or deny it, and get paid by how it arrived.
Or don’t reach him. The last screen tells you where, why, and what your last three decisions were.

sections.title: What’s in the game
list: Cars from a 16 kWh i-MiEV to a Zeekr 001, each with its own pack, connector and habits.
Real roads: the Primorye loop around Vladivostok, the M60 to Khabarovsk with its 190 km gap after Bikin, and the Amur highway to Chita, 2,155 km of it.
A real map, traced from Natural Earth, on paper that changes with the season.
Road events written separately in Russian and English, not translated.
A garage between runs, a workshop, a bag of adapters, and rent due on the first of the month.
A market that reacts, and your own asking price on the cars you sell.
A driver who gets tired and hungry, and a 12 V battery that dies at −25 °C with 60% left in the pack.

sections.title: How to play
paragraphs: Mouse or touch. On event cards the keys 1–3 pick an option, and any key skips the drive animation. On a phone, turn it sideways.
A run takes 10 to 20 minutes and the game saves on every step, so you can close the tab mid-leg and come back. English and Russian, switchable on the title screen.

punch-league.title: Punch League
punch-league.text: A boxing card battler. He shows you his next punch, and sometimes he's lying. Read him, build your combination, win three belts. Out now on Android and iPhone.
punch-league.seo_title: Punch League – boxing card battler, out now on Android, iPhone and free in your browser
punch-league.seo_description: A boxing card battler: read the card he shows, build a three-card combination, fight a career to three belts. Out now on Google Play and the App Store, the first act free in your browser.
intro: Every exchange you lay up to three cards in a chain: a setup, a punch, a finish. Your opponent has already locked his combination, and you can see the first card he is showing. Is that jab honest, or is he loading a counter? Read him, then throw.

sections.title: Combinations that mean something
list: A jab before a cross lands sharper. A body shot slows him down for the rest of the round. A block takes the initiative for your next punch.
Cards that work together light up in your hand, so you always know which combination is ready.
After the exchange the log shows what landed, what was blocked and who was first.

sections.title: A real career
list: Three acts: the local circuit, the regional ranking and the national title, a belt at the end of each.
Rivals remember you, injuries need the physio, and every night between fights is a choice: train, rest, add a card, cut a weak one, hire a coach.
Twenty-one fighters with their own decks, habits and signature punches.
Your fighter levels up and earns talents; 75 cards to collect, upgrade and merge.

sections.title: Where to play
paragraphs: The whole career is on Android, on Google Play, and on iPhone, on the App Store. Here in the browser you can play the first act, the road to your first belt.
It plays landscape, so on a phone turn it sideways. No ads, no account. English and Russian.

aerofire-command.title: AeroFire Command: Fire Season
aerofire-command.text: A wildfire is heading for town. You don't fly the helicopters: you paint the map, and your fleet does the rest. Out now on Android and iPhone, free on PC and in your browser.
aerofire-command.seo_title: AeroFire Command: Fire Season – wildfire strategy, out now on Android and iPhone, free on PC and in your browser
aerofire-command.seo_description: Paint water, retardant, firebreaks and backburns on the map and your firefighting fleet flies it. Eleven regions, seven fires a season. Out now on Google Play and the App Store, free on Windows and in the browser.
intro: Paint WATER on the flames and the helicopters fill up at the nearest lake and drop where you painted. Paint RETARDANT ahead of the fire and a tanker lays the line. Paint a CUT and the dozers dig a firebreak. Paint a BURN and a crew lights the fuel before the fire gets there. Every pilot and crew makes their own call.

sections.title: A world of fire seasons
list: Eleven regions on a living globe, from Australia and California to Greece, Turkey, Canada and Indonesia.
A season is a route of seven fires from a base town to the big one, each with its own land, wind and dryness.
Towns from a hamlet to a city edge. The star is for the houses you hold.
Fire jumped your line? Drag the beacon onto it and every aircraft piles in.

sections.title: Every fire pays in cards
list: Each star buys picks: helicopters, scoopers and tankers, hose crews, smokejumpers and dozers, parts, kits and buildings.
Sixty machines and 132 cards. The Workshop fits parts to every machine and turns one airframe into another with 98 conversions.
The Lab researches new types with the field data your fires bring in. Scores, ranks and a fire of the week.
You never lose a season: a rough fire just pays fewer cards, and your fleet comes with you.

sections.title: The fire is a simulation, not a script
paragraphs: The fire follows fuel, slope and wind. It throws embers ahead of the front, climbs ridges, crosses roads when the wind is up and turns when the wind turns. No two fires play the same.

sections.title: Where to play
paragraphs: On Android it is on Google Play, with achievements, leaderboards and cloud save; on iPhone it is on the App Store. On a computer it plays right here in the browser, or as one Windows exe from itch.io.

With a mouse: A, Z, S and X pick water, retardant, cut and burn, D is look, and holding the left button opens a wheel of the four paints. English, Russian, Spanish, Indonesian, Chinese, Turkish and Thai.

vladivostok-fortress.title: Vladivostok Fortress
vladivostok-fortress.text: A narrative strategy game about building the world's last and biggest fortress, told through an engineer officer's album from 1899.
vladivostok-fortress.seo_title: Vladivostok Fortress – narrative strategy game set in 1899
vladivostok-fortress.seo_description: A junior engineer officer in Vladivostok, 1899, builds a fortress with money he doesn’t control. A historical narrative strategy game, free in your browser.
intro: You land at Vladivostok in April 1899, forty-one days out of Odessa: a junior engineer officer with a commission, a modest salary and no authority worth the name.

Ahead of you is a ridge of forts, lunettes, batteries and redoubts, most of them still lines on a plan. Behind you is a council that sits every August, asks how much you delivered, and sets next year’s money on the answer. You will not build any of it yourself. You send other men, and find out which of them can be trusted with a work site.

sections.title: A month is a turn
paragraphs: April to October the ground takes a spade: you commit crews, buy stone, set pay, and decide whether to stand over a foreman or trust him. November to March the bay ices over, the crews scatter, and nothing rises. That is when the letters get written and the dinners get held.

sections.title: Two purses, and many people who want something
paragraphs: The crown’s money and your own are not the same money. One route is cheap virtue that everyone can see; the other is expensive vice that nobody can, until an auditor comes.

The army, the navy, the merchants and the contractors each keep their own book on you, and so do a labour contractor, a warehouse manager who is skimming, a widow from the ship out, and a staff officer who will one day be asked what happened here. Doors open by introduction, and they stay open.

sections.title: Good to know
list: Plays in the browser, best on a computer or a tablet. Nothing to install.
English and Russian.
A development build: Book I’s machinery is complete and playable end to end; the story is being written chapter by chapter.

gull-chorus.title: Gull Chorus
gull-chorus.text: Every seagull you send flies again with the next one. Lead the flock down a real beach, steal the chips, smash everything, and the whole beach plays the song.
gull-chorus.seo_title: Gull Chorus – a seagull flock that plays the song, free in your browser
gull-chorus.seo_description: Send a seagull down Bondi or a Vladivostok beach after a snack. Every gull you send flies again with the next, smashing umbrellas and bins, and the beach plays the tune. Free in your browser.
intro: Send a gull down the beach after a snack. Then send another, and the first one flies again right beside it, exactly as before. Then another. Soon you’re leading a flock of forty gulls through umbrellas, kites, wheelie bins and very annoyed picnickers, and every bump, bounce and burp is a note of the song.

sections.title: How it plays
list: Your gull chases a waving sandwich: point where to fly, down to dive and pick up speed, up to climb. Classic tap-to-flap controls are in the settings.
Let go and your gull glides down and skims along the sand. The camera keeps the beach in view and pulls back when you climb.
Skim a snack fast to snatch it in flight, or come in slow and land on the blanket.
Everything on the beach breaks. Knock a bin over and its food spills out. Bonk something sturdy and you bounce off a heart down.
Cross the finish line to end the beach for up to five stars, or keep going for more food, more smashing and more bubbles.
Every gull’s run gets a grade for its smashes, splats, near misses and high snatches. Beat the best gull of the beach.
Hold fast-forward to watch the flock go at triple speed.

sections.title: Six beaches, six songs
list: Bondi, Manly and Coogee in Sydney; Shamora, Glass Beach and Tokarevsky Lighthouse in Vladivostok, each with its own gulls and its own snacks.
Every beach plays a classic tune on real instruments: Waltzing Matilda at Bondi, the Wellerman at Manly, Kalinka at Shamora and more.
The song grows with the flock: new sections, more instruments, a key change, so gull twenty-five never sounds like gull five.
Every few gulls something turns up on the beach: an ice-cream van, a wedding party, a fishing boat unloading, a lifeguard. More food, and more to smash.
The whole beach bobs to the beat, and the sky and the sea change colour with the song.
Finish a beach and the whole flock comes back as a gull tsunami that smashes the melody out of whatever is still standing.

sections.title: Special gulls
paragraphs: Stars buy special gulls: Fatso with extra hearts, the Gobbler who swallows two snacks in one gulp, the Phantom who flies straight through things, Kaboom, the Seagull King and more. Each has a few goes per beach, so pick your moment.

sections.title: Where to play
paragraphs: Free in your browser, here or on itch.io, and as a Windows download. Mouse, keyboard or touch: on a phone, drag to steer. In English.

souls-and-estates.title: Souls & Estates
souls-and-estates.text: Head a Russian noble house until serfdom ends in 1861. Set what each serf village owes, lay out the land, hear the elders, winter in Moscow and climb the Table of Ranks.
souls-and-estates.seo_title: Souls & Estates – run a Russian noble estate until 1861, free in your browser
souls-and-estates.seo_description: A strategy game about a Russian noble house: set rent or labour for each serf village, place the mill and the smithy, hear the village elders, marry well and climb the Table of Ranks until serfdom ends in 1861. In English and Russian, free in your browser and on Windows.
intro: You don’t chop the wood. You own the people who chop the wood, and the Crown counts your wealth in souls. Run a country estate the way a landowner did, through a steward, bailiffs, village elders and letters, season after season until serfdom is abolished on 19 February 1861.

sections.title: What you do
list: Start in 1670, 1700 or 1762, each with the prices, laws and history of its day, and play on to 1861.
Set each village’s terms: rent in money, or days of labour on the manor’s fields. Every option shows the rubles a year and how the village will take it before you choose.
Plough, plant, set out orchards and found new villages. Fields grow in rings of strips round each village and reach only as far as people can walk.
Lay out the land yourself: put the mill on the river, the smithy by the road and the barns where you like, inside each village’s bounds. Out of room? Move a house.
Turn the mouse wheel to go from one family’s yard to the whole estate, then the district as a table of miniatures, then a map table of central Russia.
Hear the village elders: seed loans, a medic looking for a place, passes for winter work in town.
Pay the poll tax on every name on the census list, living or dead, until the next count.
Send sons into the Guards or the civil service, marry daughters well, winter in Moscow or Petersburg, and build the family nest.

sections.title: The art book
paragraphs: A free 30-page art book is on the itch page: the estate in four seasons, the model kit, the interface’s six seasonal inks and three typefaces, every screen, the history behind the numbers and the looks we threw away.

sections.title: Where to play
paragraphs: In your browser right here, or download the Windows build from itch.io. Desktop only, mouse and keyboard. English and Russian, switchable in the settings. The game is in development (version 0.104).

orbital-jump.title: Orbital Jump Reloaded
orbital-jump.text: The 2021 planet-hopper rebuilt: ten worlds, a wall of fire behind you, items for a bad moment, five suits and the classic endless run. Out now on Android and iPhone, free in your browser.
orbital-jump.seo_title: Orbital Jump Reloaded – one-button space runner, out on Android and iPhone, free in your browser
orbital-jump.seo_description: Run around a planet, jump to the next one and stay ahead of the burning Sun. Ten worlds, black holes, wormholes, predator planets, five suits and an endless mode. Free on Google Play, the App Store and in your browser, no ads.
intro: Your astronaut runs around a planet. Click, tap or press Space to jump off it, fly to the next one, land, and go again. Keep moving: the Sun behind you has caught fire, and it is coming.

sections.title: A galaxy to cross
list: Ten worlds in two galaxies: Earth, the Moon, Mars, Venus, Europa and Titan, then on into Andromeda. Every world is a chain of short missions: collect the stars and the spheres, reach the beacon, and the next one opens.
There is no set path. Every flight is your timing, your launch and the pull of the planets around you. Chain clean landings for combos and Space Coins.
Black holes swallow you whole. Wormholes throw you across the sky. Predator planets hunt you down. Asteroids, alien ships, and a wall of fire that never stops.
Three items for a bad moment: a time slowdown that holds the Sun to half speed, an energy elixir, a life capsule. Rare Star and Orb magnets pull the pickups to you.
Five suits with their own trails, glows and landing sparks. Looks only, never an advantage.
Finish Earth and the classic endless run opens: drill soil on every planet, build gadgets in the Hangar, fly the daily galaxy that is the same for everyone.

sections.title: Where to play
paragraphs: The whole game is on Android, on Google Play, and on iPhone, on the App Store: free, no ads, no timers. You earn Space Coins by playing; coin packs are there for a head start and never needed to finish a world.
Here in the browser it is the same game with a test shop. Left mouse button, Space, W or the up arrow jumps; 1, 2, 3 use the items; Esc or P pauses; on a phone, tap. English and Russian.

Made by the VRLab team in Vladivostok in 2021: Aleksei Rezepov (idea, design, art, effects), Alexandr Krivobokov (code), Maxim Moskalenko (music and sound), Evgeny Andreev (planets and illustrations), Igor Matievskii and Daniil Zimenkov. Rebuilt by Golden Harbour Games in 2026. The original is still playable on itch.io.

roach-invasion.title: Roach Invasion
roach-invasion.text: You are one small cockroach in a huge kitchen. Grab the crumbs, run them home to the colony, and don’t be under the slipper when it comes down.
roach-invasion.seo_title: Roach Invasion – a cockroach’s kitchen raid, free in your browser
roach-invasion.seo_description: One small cockroach, a huge kitchen and giant humans who don’t want you there. Grab the food, dodge the slipper, the vacuum and the cat, and grow the colony. An early build, free in your browser and as an Android APK.
intro: There are crumbs on the floor, a colony waiting under the floorboards, and giant humans who really don’t want you here. Grab the food, run it home, and stay out from under the slipper.

sections.title: How it plays
list: Danger shows on the floor first. A red ring marks where a foot, a slipper or a mop is about to land. Step out of it and you’re fine.
A full bag is a slow bag. The more you carry, the slower you run. Drop it off at the nest, or push your luck for one more crumb.
Holes save lives. Duck into a shelter and wait for the vacuum or the torch to pass.
Grow the colony. Spend the food on bigger bags, a running track and a faster dash, then dig the tunnel into the apartment.

sections.title: What’s in it
list: Six kitchen raids: some against the clock, one with two nests to fill, and one that ends with an escape through the vent.
Two apartment rooms: the canyon under the sofa, and a night corridor with a torch sweeping the floor.
The Big Cookie: drag home a cookie bigger than you, with Pip pulling alongside.
The Cat Woke Up: a huge cat wakes mid-raid. Freeze, hide, or rustle a bag to make it look away. If it spots you, run for a hole.
Pip, the colony’s first little one, who joins your raids and carries a crumb in his backpack.

sections.title: Where to play
paragraphs: Here in the browser, or as an Android APK from itch.io. On a phone the left thumb runs and the right button dashes; on a computer use WASD or the arrow keys, Space to dash, E for the action button and Esc to pause.
An early build that is still growing: new rooms are on the way. In English and Russian, switchable in the settings. Made by Golden Harbour Games in Sydney together with VR Lab in Vladivostok.

about.title: Two harbours
paragraphs: Vladivostok sits on the Golden Horn, a bay named after Istanbul's. Sydney sits on Port Jackson. Both are harbour cities with a famous bridge across the water, and the studio is named for the pair of them.

Our games come from both places: the roads, forts and weather of the Russian Far East, and the bushfire country around Sydney. They run on Android, iPhone, Windows and in a browser, and you can play them all free: right here, on Google Play, on the App Store or on itch.io.
about.mission: Make small, sharp games about real things, and treat the people who play them as grown-ups.
about.vision: A studio where a two-person idea can become a finished, polished game in months, where every game plays free in a browser for anyone, anywhere, and where the money a game earns goes back into making that game better and more human.
promises: Every game plays free in your browser. No account, no install, no card.
No energy timers, no loot boxes, no dark patterns. A purchase, where there is one, is a thank-you, a cosmetic or a head start, never a wall across the story.
Your data is not the product. The games collect nothing they do not need; the privacy page says exactly what, in plain words.
When you tell us something is wrong, we fix it. The harbour log on the home page is where you can see it happen.
We tell you what is made by a machine and what is made by a person. Always.
letter: Honestly? Better than a week ago, and still worse than we would like. Eight games are in port, and three of them are now on both Google Play and the App Store: Fire Season, Punch League and Orbital Jump Reloaded, the rebuild of our 2021 phone game. Apple sent Punch League back with questions the first time and passed it the second.

The numbers are small. Our YouTube channel has passed thirty-six thousand views across a hundred or so short films, mostly about firefighting helicopters, Russian serfs, and things we got wrong and then fixed. Downloads are in the hundreds, not the thousands. Nobody has quit a day job. That is fine. This is a long voyage and the boat floats.

What is working: shipping, and listening. We took Souls & Estates to a developers’ meetup and were told, kindly, that there was too much to read and too many Russian words. Within two days every screen had icons and the terms were plain English. The same week the game learned to zoom from one village yard out to a map table of central Russia.

What is not working yet: being found. Eight good small games nobody has heard of are still eight games nobody has heard of. So we post every day, we answer every comment, and we keep pages like this one so that people who care how games get made can see how ours are.

Next: Souls & Estates gets a tutorial that opens its menus one step at a time; Fire Season gets a tutorial that does not need a manual; Punch League is learning to fight in 3D; the experiments get a page and a forum of their own; and the first human artist gets hired the month a game pays for one.

privacy.title: Privacy policy
privacy.description: How Golden Harbour Games handles your data: two games send anonymous play data and offer an optional Google Play Games sign-in, the rest collect none, and this website sets no cookies of its own.
intro: Golden Harbour Games Pty Ltd is a small game studio in Sydney, Australia. This page explains what we do with your data, which is very little. It covers all our games and apps, wherever you get them — Google Play, the App Store, itch.io, Steam or this website — and the website itself.

sections.title: Our games
list: Our games need no account. Nothing is required to sign up for or log in to. AeroFire Command: Fire Season and Punch League offer an optional Google Play Games sign-in, described below; you can play the whole game without it.
They contain no ads and no advertising tracking.

Most of our games collect no data at all, Orbital Jump Reloaded on both stores included. AeroFire Command: Fire Season and Punch League on Android (the versions from Google Play) are the exceptions: they send anonymous play data, described in the next section. Their iPhone versions from the App Store send us nothing and have no Google sign-in.

On iPhone, Fire Season and Orbital Jump Reloaded can post your scores and achievements to Apple’s Game Center, if you are signed in to Game Center on your device. That goes to Apple, under your own Game Center settings; nothing comes to us.

Game progress is saved on your own device. If you sign in to Google Play Games in Fire Season or Punch League, a copy of your career is also kept in your Google account, as described below. We never hold a copy ourselves.

sections.title: Anonymous play data in AeroFire Command: Fire Season and Punch League
paragraphs: To learn how our games play - where new players get stuck, how long a fire or a fight takes, which cards people pick, how smoothly the game runs - Fire Season and Punch League send anonymous play events to Google Analytics for Firebase. For example: a fire or a fight started or finished and its result, a tutorial step reached, a card picked, a belt won, a look in the shop viewed or bought, a setting changed, the frame rate.

Each install gets a random ID that the game makes up on first launch. It is not linked to your name, email address, Google account, Play Games profile or advertising ID, and the games do not collect the advertising ID. Nothing you type is sent. Firebase also records standard technical details: device model, Android version, country, language and app version.
Google processes this data for us under the Google Analytics terms and keeps it for up to 14 months. It is not used for advertising, and we do not sell or share it.
You can turn it off at any time in the game's SETTINGS: "Share anonymous play data" in Fire Season, "SHARE PLAY DATA" in Punch League. From then on the game sends nothing.

sections.title: Google Play Games in AeroFire Command: Fire Season and Punch League
paragraphs: Fire Season and Punch League can sign you in to Google Play Games, if you choose to, from SETTINGS. Signing in gives you achievements, leaderboards and a cloud copy of your career. You never have to sign in to play.

When you sign in, Google Play Games gives the game your Play Games player ID and the display name and avatar you chose for Play Games. The game uses them to show your name on the leaderboards and to tell which saved game is yours. It does not receive your email address or your Google account name, and it never puts your Play Games name or ID in the anonymous play data.

Your achievements and scores are sent to Google Play Games, where they appear under your Play Games profile according to the visibility you chose there. Your saved career (in Fire Season the season, the fleet, the records and settings; in Punch League your fighters, record, belts, deck and the looks you own) is kept in your Google account's saved-games storage, not on any server of ours, and only that game can read it. Signing out, or clearing the game's data in Google Play Games, removes it.
Google processes this data under the Google Play Games terms and the Google privacy policy. We do not sell or share it, and we do not use it for advertising.

sections.title: This website
paragraphs: goldenharbourgames.com is a static site: plain pages, no sign-in, no forms. It sets no cookies of its own. If you pick a language, the page remembers that choice in your browser only; nothing is sent anywhere.

The site is hosted on GitHub Pages. GitHub's servers may log standard request data, such as your IP address and browser user agent, as described in GitHub's privacy statement. Our pages load their typefaces from Google Fonts, so your browser also requests those from Google's servers, under Google's privacy policy.
When you press Play on a game page, the game loads in a frame from itch.io. Inside that frame, itch.io's privacy policy applies.

The forum linked from the Experiments pages is GitHub Discussions. It lives on github.com, and reading or posting there falls under GitHub’s privacy statement. Where a page offers to show a thread’s comments in place, pressing that button loads them through giscus (giscus.app), an open-source comment widget; nothing is requested from giscus or GitHub until you press it.

sections.title: Stores
paragraphs: Google Play, the App Store, RuStore, itch.io and Steam handle purchases, downloads and installs. What they collect when you buy or install a game is governed by their own privacy policies, not by us.

Where a game offers an optional purchase, the store you play through handles the payment: the Supporter edition of Fire Season; the shop’s looks in Punch League (outfits and card backs that change nothing in a fight; the Full Career purchase sold from 13 to 24 October 2026 is still restored for those who bought it); and the Space Coin packs and the Welcome Bundle in Orbital Jump Reloaded. The game only learns whether a purchase went through, so it can give you what you bought. Your payment details never reach us.

sections.title: Children
paragraphs: Our games are not directed at children under 13. We knowingly collect no data from anyone, children included.

sections.title: If this changes
paragraphs: If we ever add anything that touches your data — an account, online features, analytics, a store inside a game — we will update this page and the store listings before shipping it, and say what changed.

sections.title: Contact
paragraphs: Questions about this policy or about your data: write to us.

terms.title: Terms of service
terms.seo_title: Terms of Service · Golden Harbour Games
terms.description: The terms for playing Golden Harbour Games games and buying their optional extras: what you may do with them, how purchases and refunds work, and your rights under consumer law.
intro: Golden Harbour Games Pty Ltd is a small game studio in Sydney, Australia. These terms apply when you play any of our games or apps, wherever you got them (Google Play, the App Store, itch.io, Steam or this website), and when you buy something inside them. By playing, you agree to them. The short version: the games are yours to enjoy, purchases are handled by the store you use, and nothing here takes away your rights under consumer law.

sections.title: Who we are
paragraphs: The games are made and published by Golden Harbour Games Pty Ltd, Sydney, New South Wales, Australia. We make games as a business, so we are a trader under consumer law.

sections.title: Playing our games
list: We give you a personal, non-exclusive, non-transferable licence to install and play our games on your own devices for your own enjoyment. The games, their art, music, words and code remain ours or our licensors’.
Please don’t copy, resell or redistribute the games, take them apart to reuse their parts, or cheat in ways that affect other players (for example on leaderboards).
You are welcome to stream our games and post videos and screenshots of them, including on channels that earn money. A link back to the game is appreciated but not required.
If you are under 18, please ask a parent or guardian before buying anything in a game.

sections.title: Optional purchases
paragraphs: Our games are free to play in full. Some offer optional purchases. In AeroFire Command: Fire Season it is the Supporter edition, and in Punch League the shop’s looks (outfits and card backs): they change how things look and support the studio, and never make you stronger in play. Orbital Jump Reloaded sells packs of Space Coins, its in-game currency, and a one-time Welcome Bundle. Space Coins are also earned by playing; they buy suits and helper items, and every world can be finished without buying any. Space Coins have no cash value and cannot be exchanged or transferred.

Purchases are sold and processed by the store you play through, such as Google Play or the App Store, under that store’s terms. The price is shown in the store’s own payment sheet before you pay, in your local currency and including any taxes the store must charge.

A one-time purchase (the Supporter edition, a look in Punch League) is linked to your store account: if you reinstall the game, or play on another device signed in to the same account, the game restores it. Space Coins and what you buy with them in Orbital Jump Reloaded are kept in the game’s save on your device and do not move to a new install. Items you bought stay yours across updates.

sections.title: Refunds and your consumer rights
paragraphs: Refunds are handled by the store you bought from, under its refund policy; ask them first, as they hold the payment. If something you bought does not work, write to us too and we will help.

Nothing in these terms limits rights you have under the law where you live. If you are in Australia, our games come with guarantees under the Australian Consumer Law that cannot be excluded. If you are in the European Union or the United Kingdom, you keep your statutory rights for digital content; when you buy digital content that is delivered straight away, the store will ask you to agree to immediate delivery, which ends the 14-day right of withdrawal once the content is delivered.

sections.title: Updates and changes
paragraphs: We keep improving our games, so updates may add, change or remove features. We may stop offering a game in a store in the future. If we change these terms, we will update this page and its date; changes apply from that date and never take away something you already bought.

sections.title: Other services
paragraphs: Some games use services run by others: Google Play Games and Apple’s Game Center for the optional sign-in, achievements, leaderboards and cloud saves, and the stores for purchases. Their own terms apply to those parts. The forum linked from this site is GitHub Discussions, under GitHub’s terms. On the App Store, Apple’s standard Licensed Application End User License Agreement also applies; where it and these terms differ, these terms apply between you and us. How our games handle data is set out in our privacy policy.

sections.title: Warranty and liability
paragraphs: We work hard to make our games run well, but we cannot promise they will be free of every bug or work on every device. To the extent the law allows, the games are provided as they are, and we are not liable for indirect or consequential loss. Where the law does not allow us to exclude a guarantee or limit our liability, these terms do not try to.

sections.title: Governing law
paragraphs: These terms are governed by the laws of New South Wales, Australia. If you are a consumer living elsewhere, you also keep the protection of the mandatory laws of your own country, and you can bring a claim in your local courts.

sections.title: Contact
paragraphs: Questions about these terms, a purchase, or anything else: write to us.

facts: Sydney, Australia; roots in Vladivostok, Russia
Android (Google Play, RuStore), iPhone (App Store), Windows, browser
boilerplate: Golden Harbour Games is an independent studio between two harbours: the Golden Horn in Vladivostok, where its founders grew up, and Sydney Harbour, where it makes games now. It makes small, sharp games with a real subject behind each one: wildfire aviation, boxing, the Russian serf estate, a used electric car across Siberia.

Every game plays free in the browser; the phone games are on Google Play and the App Store. The studio writes and voices its games in English and Russian, and some in five more languages. It also experiments in the open with VR, AR and robots.

build.title: Built with AI. Steered by people.
build.lede: We say it out loud: most of what you see here was made with AI tools, by a studio of two that could not have made it any other way. Here is exactly who does what.
build.manifest_note: Roughly how the work splits across our games today. Hover or tap a line for the detail.

rows.name: Design and rules
rows.note: Every mechanic is argued over at a kitchen table and on a phone in a bus. AI drafts options; we pick, cut and tune. The feel is ours.

rows.name: Play-testing
rows.note: A phone in a hand, headless simulations by the hundred, and friends who tell us the truth. No model plays a game for fun.

rows.name: Writing
rows.note: Briefs, jokes and the history behind the games come from us; AI drafts the long text and the seven languages, and we read every line.

rows.name: Code
rows.note: Claude writes most of it; we read it, test it, break it, and decide what ships. Thousands of automated checks run before a build goes out.

rows.name: Art and covers
rows.note: Gemini and hand fixes. Some pieces we are proud of; some we know are not there yet. See the promise below.

rows.name: Music and sound
rows.note: ElevenLabs makes the scores and the effects to our briefs. We pick, cut and mix.

rows.name: Voices
rows.note: Radio chatter in seven languages, boxing corners, village elders: generated, then listened to by a native speaker where we have one.

paragraphs: Why so much AI? Because the alternative was no games at all. Two people, no budget and a list of games we wanted to exist. With these tools a season of wildfires, a boxing career, a serf village over a hundred years and a road across Siberia could be built, played and shipped by a crew that fits in one car.

What AI is good at: the first draft of anything, and the thousandth. Code, a thousand radio lines, a cover in an hour instead of a week. What it is bad at: knowing what is fun, knowing when to stop, and caring. Those stay with us. Every mechanic is played until it earns its place. Every sentence you read was read by a person first.
We do not hide any of this in the credits and we never will. If a part of a game was generated, it says so. If you ask which part, we will tell you.
build.promise: When a game earns enough, we rebuild its generated parts with people: artists for the covers and the worlds, composers for the scores, actors for the voices, writers for the words. Their names go on the game. The first game to pay for itself will be the first to get its crew.

crew.title: Game development internships and open projects
crew.seo_title: Game development internships and open projects (remote) · Golden Harbour Games
crew.description: Work on real, released indie games, remotely. Students can do a course placement in game design, programming, art or sound; anyone can take an open project as an independent contributor, for credit and a share of the game’s revenue.
crew.lede: Work on real games that are already on the App Store and Google Play. Pick a game, make one part of it better, and put your name in its credits.
get: Your work in a released game, in front of real players.
Your name in the credits of the game and on this site.
Something finished for your portfolio: a level, a character, a soundtrack, a feature, a language.
The full source code and our tools, including the AI tools we build with, and one of us in a chat when you are stuck.
A share of the game’s revenue for open projects, agreed in writing before you start.
how: Choose a game and the part you want to work on. The open projects are listed here; your own idea is welcome too.
Email us. Say what you would like to do and show us anything you have made, finished or not. We answer within a few days.
We put it in writing: what the project is, what finished looks like, who owns the work and what your share is.
You work remotely, when it suits you. Most projects are a few weeks of spare time.
Your work ships in the game, with your name on it.
crew.who: Students, graduates, career changers and self-taught beginners, anywhere in the world. Game designers, programmers (we use Godot and Unity), 2D and 3D artists, animators, composers and sound designers, writers, translators, voice actors and testers. You do not need a degree or a portfolio. You need to care about one of these games enough to make one part of it better.
crew.closing: No form and no deadline. One email is enough to start.
faq: An open project pays a share of the game’s revenue, agreed in writing before you start, plus credit. There is no wage and nothing up front. Our games earn little so far, and we will tell you the real numbers in the first email. You never pay us anything.
Only if your course requires a placement and your school arranges it with us. Everything else on this page is an open project: you are an independent contributor, not an intern and not an employee.
Yes, fully. The studio is in Sydney, Australia, and we work with people in any time zone. Everything happens over email, chat and the shared project.
How much time does it take?
That is up to you. We agree on the result, not on hours. Most people fit a project around study or a job.
No. We care more about what you want to make than about what you have done.
Godot 4 and Unity for the games, Blender for 3D, GitHub for everything, and AI tools such as Claude for code and first drafts. You get access to all of it.

It becomes part of the game, so the studio needs the right to ship and keep it. The agreement says so in plain words, along with your credit and your share. You can always show the work in your portfolio.
Any time. There are no intakes and no deadline. Email us and we go from there.

oars.text: Level design: a new region on the globe, with its own trees, wind and fires.
Character art and voice: portraits for a second season of fighters, and a corner voice for each.
Sound and writing: village songs and a church bell; proofreading of the Russian edition.
Level design and music: a new beach with its own tune.
Writing: a road event you have lived through on a real road.
Testing: play the game on your phone and tell us where it bores you.
Level design and art: a new apartment room with a danger of its own.
VR, AR and robots: an experiment of your own, with our hardware notes and help.
Translation: any language we do not have yet, for any game.

ways: For anyone, anywhere. You take one project as an independent contributor: you choose it, you work in your own time on your own equipment, and you are paid a share of what the game earns, under a written agreement.
If your course requires a placement, we can host it. It is arranged with your school, follows its rules on hours, supervision and reports, and is built around what you need to learn.
crew.status_note: An open project is not a job and not employment. Nobody sets your hours, and you are free to work for anyone else at the same time.

creed.title: Games first
creed.lede: We were players long before we were a studio. Four things we hold ourselves to.

items.title: We make games we love
items.text: Every game here began as something one of us wanted to play and could not find. If we would not play it on our own phone on the train home, it does not ship.

items.title: Good for everyone
items.text: No manual, no account, no wall across the story. A child, a parent and someone with thirty years of strategy games behind them should all find their way in within a minute.

items.title: We stay with our games
items.text: A release is a start, not a finish. New builds go out most weeks, the log below shows what changed, and what players tell us goes into the next one.

items.title: We experiment
items.text: VR, AR, a robot on the desk, a game inside a Reddit post. We try new hardware and odd ideas to find ways of playing that do not exist yet, and we show the results, good or not.

studio.description: Who makes Golden Harbour Games: two harbours, what we promise players, how the games are built by people and AI, and an honest note on how it is going.

experiments.description: What Golden Harbour Games tries outside its shipped games: a VR storm at sea, a wildfire on a table, AR models, humanoid robots and new places for a game to live. Write-ups, pictures and an open forum.
experiments.lede: This is the workshop. We use VR, AR and whatever else turns up to look for new ways to play. Each experiment has a write-up, pictures and a thread where you can tell us what you think.
experiments.talk_text: Questions, ideas, “you should try this instead”: the thread for this experiment is open to anyone.
experiments.forum_text: One place to talk to us and to each other: ideas for the games, bugs, your own experiments, anything at all. Every experiment has a thread of its own, and you can start a new one.
